The JWT, rotation and blacklisting sections still stand; doc 04 remains authoritative for the endpoint surface.

Design spec for the auth stack. Tokens and type scale come from doc 12. Interactive version: Omelette project `Macros Tracker Native setup`, `Macros Tracker App.dc.html`, options **6a–6d** — one state machine, all transitions live.

Four states: `welcome → email (register | login) → verify`, plus `reset` reachable from login.

## Welcome (6a)

Wordmark set at 46px/900 with an accent dot, then one line of positioning: `A photo and a sentence. That's the whole log.` Nothing else competes.

Button order, top to bottom:

1. **Sign in with Apple** — white fill, black text, Apple's own styling
2. **Continue with email** — hairline outline
3. **Already have an account? Log in** — mono text link

Apple takes the top slot for two reasons: guideline 4.8 requires an equivalent privacy-preserving option once any third-party login exists, and it removes password friction entirely on the platform this ships to first.

**The AI disclosure lives here, not in settings:**

> Your food photos are sent to an AI provider to estimate macros. Nothing is shared with anyone else.

Reviewers look for this, and a user deserves to know before they sign up rather than after.

## Register / log in (6b)

**One screen, two modes.** The fields are identical, so a second screen would be duplication. A mono segmented control switches `REGISTER` / `LOG IN`, and the heading follows (`Create an account` / `Welcome back`).

* Email and password fields, 10px radius, surface fill, hairline border
* `SHOW` / `HIDE` toggle on the password label — not an icon, a word
* **Register mode** grows three password rules as dot + text rows, greyed until satisfied. These mirror Django's default validators; do not invent a stricter minimum
* **Login mode** grows `FORGOT YOUR PASSWORD?`
* Footer, permanently visible: `Login, register and reset are all rate limited by address and by IP.`

Naming the rate limit in the UI is deliberate — it sets expectations before someone hits it and thinks the app is broken.

## Verify email (6c)

A **blocking** step, stated once and plainly rather than nagged:

> We sent a link to [alex@hintology.com](<mailto:alex@hintology.com>)
> Tap it and you'll land back here, verified. Until then you can't log food — the account isn't real yet.

Three rows in a grouped list: `Open mail app` · `Resend the link` (with a visible `IN 42s` cooldown) · `Use a different address`.

The cooldown is shown rather than hidden behind a disabled button. Footer: `Resend is throttled. A cooldown is cheaper than a mail provider blocking us.`

## Password reset (6d)

Email field, and an inline note for whoever builds it:

> The next screen says *a link has been sent* whether or not that address has an account. Confirming which emails exist is a free gift to anyone enumerating users.

Per doc 04 the response must be identical in both cases. This is a correctness requirement, not a nicety, so it is stated on the screen itself.

## Not screens, but part of this epic

* **Sign in with Apple, first authorization only.** Apple returns name and email exactly once. Persist immediately or lose it forever. Join on `apple_user_id` (the stable subject claim), never on email — users may relay a private address
* **Token storage** — `expo-secure-store`, Keychain-backed. Never AsyncStorage
* **Global 401 handler** wired into the React Query client, not per-call: attempt one refresh, retry the request, and on failure clear storage and route to Welcome. Doing it per-call is how apps end up with inconsistent logout behaviour
* **Account deletion** lives in settings, not here. Soft delete, tokens blacklisted immediately, R2 objects queued, hard purge after 30 days

## Routing after auth

```
Launch
  → token in secure store?
      no  → Welcome
      yes → valid? → email verified? → onboarding complete?
                                          no  → Onboarding
                                          yes → Home
```
